parts.text:
**"The Mom Test"** is a framework for conducting customer interviews, popularized by author and entrepreneur Rob Fitzpatrick in his highly influential book, *The Mom Test: How to talk to customers and learn if your business is a good idea when everyone is lying to you*. 

In the startup and product management worlds, it is widely considered the gold standard for validating business ideas.

---

### The Core Problem It Solves
When you have a new business idea, your natural instinct is to ask friends, family, or potential customers: *"Hey, I have this idea. What do you think of it? Would you buy it?"*

Most people are polite and want to encourage you, so they will say: *"That’s a great idea! I would definitely use that!"* This is called **false validation**. You walk away feeling confident, spend months and thousands of dollars building the product, only to launch it and find that absolutely nobody actually wants to buy it. 

The book is called "The Mom Test" because **even your mom, who loves you and wants to protect your feelings, won't be able to lie to you if you ask the right questions**.

---

### The 3 Rules of the Mom Test
To pass the Mom Test and get brutally honest, useful feedback, you must follow three simple rules:

#### 1. Talk about their life, not your idea
Do not pitch your product. In fact, if possible, **do not even mention that you have an idea**. The moment people know you are building something, they will start filtering their answers to be supportive. Instead, ask them about their daily lives, their current workflows, and the frustrations they actively face.
*   **Bad:** *"I’m building an app that helps you track your diet. Do you think you'd use that?"*
*   **Good:** *"How do you currently try to stay healthy? What’s the hardest part about managing your diet?"*

#### 2. Ask about specifics in the past, not hypotheticals about the future
Humans are incredibly bad at predicting their future behavior, but they are highly reliable when reporting past actions. Never ask "Would you..." or "How often would you...". Always ask "When was the last time you..." or "How did you solve...".
*   **Bad:** *"Would you pay $10 a month for a tool that organizes your closet?"*
*   **Good:** *"The last time you cleaned out your closet, what did you do? Have you ever bought any closet organizers? If so, what did they cost?"*

#### 3. Talk less, listen more
Your job in a customer interview is not to sell, convince, or defend your idea. Your job is to listen. When you speak, you bias the customer. Let them do 80% of the talking, and dig deeper into their pain points with simple follow-ups like *"Why do you say that?"* or *"Can you walk me through the last time that happened?"*

---

### Good Questions vs. Bad Questions

| Bad (Hypothetical & Opinion-Based) | Good (Action & Fact-Based) |
| :--- | :--- |
| "Do you think this is a good idea?" | "How do you currently solve this problem?" |
| "Would you buy a product that did X?" | "What are you currently doing/paying to fix X?" |
| "How much would you pay for this?" | "The last time you ran into this, what did you do?" |
| "Don't you think this feature is cool?" | "How does that problem affect the rest of your day?" |
| "Would you use an app for that?" | "Walk me through your current workflow for this task." |

### Why This Matters
If you ask the "good" questions, you will quickly discover whether the problem you are trying to solve is actually a **pain point** that people care enough about to pay for, or if it's just a minor inconvenience they have no interest in solving. The Mom Test ensures you base your business on **real human behavior** rather than polite, empty promises.
